posts.title: The Discipline of Handwork: Inside a Training Day at Lindmoor
posts.excerpt: At Kesho College, future salon juniors build professional confidence through daily tutor demonstrations, mannequin drills, and supervised floor work with real clients.
posts.content:
Every morning at 08:45, the training floor at 14 Harbour Lane in Lindmoor opens with quiet, deliberate preparation. Mirrors are cleaned, shears and sectioning combs are laid across workbenches, and stations are arranged before the first demonstration begins. Founded in 2009 by colour specialist Amara Lindqvist, Kesho College was built around a straightforward belief: hairdressing cannot be mastered through distant observation or abstract textbook diagrams. It is an exacting manual craft that must be absorbed through hands-on repetition, standing beside mentors who perform the work every day.

At 09:00, the entire cohort gathers in a semicircle around the central demonstration chair. Head of cutting Theo Marchetti or founder Amara Lindqvist leads the session, demonstrating a single technical process in complete detail. Whether breaking down the geometric elevation of a graduated bob, refining the hand tension needed for a blunt perimeter, or calculating foil placement for multidimensional colour, the instructor explains each step out loud. Students watch finger angles, body balance, and blade travel up close. There are no rushed shortcuts or theatrical flourishes; the focus remains entirely on clean lines, steady posture, and deliberate blade control.

By 10:15, students transition to their own stations for mannequin block practice. Each trainee repeats the demonstrated cut or foil pattern on high-density practice heads, translating visual observation into muscle memory. Because cohorts are strictly capped at 14 learners, instructors move continuously along the benches, adjusting a student's thumb position, correcting comb angles, and pointing out uneven sectioning before bad habits can settle in. This intense repetition on mannequins provides a safe, disciplined space where mistakes are caught and corrected immediately, ensuring students understand why a technique succeeds or fails.

Following a one-hour lunch break at 12:30, the rhythm of the college shifts decisively. At 13:30, our Student Salon opens its doors to the public, welcoming local clients who have booked appointments for an €18 cut and finish, colour services starting from €35, or a €10 beard trim. This live client floor is where classroom theory meets commercial reality. Students greet their clients, conduct thorough consultations, wash hair, formulate colour shades, and execute cuts under the watchful eye of instructors maintaining a strict 1:7 supervision ratio. Tutors check every perimeter line, verify colour balance, and guide student communication before any client leaves.

The day concludes at 16:15 with an honest group critique led by the teaching team. Students gather around finished mannequin heads and discuss the client services delivered that afternoon, sharing practical difficulties, technical triumphs, and customer service insights. Tools are then cleaned, blades oiled, towels laundered, and workstations sanitised before the building closes at 17:00. This disciplined thirty-hour weekly cycle builds more than technical skill; it develops the stamina, punctuality, and professional resilience essential for long-term salon careers.

For aspiring stylists aged 16 and older preparing to enter the trade, this daily structure offers an authentic bridge into commercial employment. From our initial four-step admissions process and monthly open mornings to the final practical assessments of the 12-month Hairdressing Diploma, Kesho College remains dedicated to deliberate craft. By learning step by step from working stylists, students leave our Harbour Lane campus equipped with the quiet confidence, technical discipline, and practical capability that modern salon owners value most.
